title: The Attacker Moves Second: Stronger Adaptive Attacks Bypass Defenses Against Llm Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections
titleEn: Paper proposes adaptive attack framework that breaks through 12 LLM jailbreak and prompt injection defenses
summary: The paper "The Attacker Moves Second" argues that current LLM defense evaluations often rely on static attack strings or weak optimization methods not designed against the defenses, thus overestimating robustness. The authors adaptively adjust attack strategies using four methods—gradient descent, reinforcement learning, random search, and human red teaming—achieving attack success rates mostly above 90% on 12 recent defenses, whereas the original papers reported values mostly near zero. On AgentDojo, Spotlighting and Prompt Sandwiching had attack success rates as low as 1% under static attacks, but both exceeded 95% when switched to search-based adaptive attacks; MetaSecAlign rose from 2% on the static benchmark to 96%; an RL attack against Circuit Breakers reached 100% on HarmBench. Based on this, the authors propose four lessons: small static evaluations are misleading, automated evaluation is effective but insufficient to guarantee robustness, human red teaming remains the most effective, and model-based automatic scorers themselves can be adversarially attacked.

parts.text: Existing evaluations of defenses against large model jailbreak and prompt injection mostly use static harmful prompts or low-compute weak optimization methods that are not adapted to the defenses, and thus cannot accurately reflect the true performance of defenses against strong attackers with targeted designs.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: The authors propose a unified adaptive attack framework (propose, score, select, update loop) and instantiate it as four types of adaptive attacks: gradient-based, reinforcement learning (GRPO optimization), search-based (MAP Elites with large model mutation), and human red team.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: The authors evaluate 12 recent defenses, with adaptive attacks achieving ASR above 90% on most defenses; in selected AgentDojo scenarios, the human red team achieved attacks in all tested scenarios (ASR reaching 100%).
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The experiments skipped planning-execution defenses where control flow is completely independent of data; the performance of automated search under multiple independent restarts was not reported; the LLM-based judge itself is susceptible to adversarial examples and reward hacking.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: ASPI: Seeking Ambiguity Clarification Amplifies Prompt Injection Vulnerability in LLM Agents
titleEn: ASPI benchmark: prompt injection attack success rate rises substantially when agents seek clarification
summary: The researchers propose the ASPI benchmark and find that LLM agents' vulnerability to prompt injection increases significantly after switching from standard execution to a clarification-seeking state. The benchmark builds 728 task-attack pairs based on AgentDojo, covering four domains—Workspace, Slack, Travel, and Banking—and keeps the task, attack goal, environment, and scoring fixed while varying only the interaction state and delivery channel. Across ten frontier models, attack success rates generally increase from the execution state to the clarification state; for example, o3 rises from 1.8% to 34.0%, Gemini-3-Flash from 2.2% to 35.7%, and Kimi K2.5 from 11.1% to 63.1%, while Claude-Opus-4.7 remains near zero in both settings. Decomposition analysis shows that the ask_user clarification channel is the main source of increased vulnerability, while the effect of the interaction state itself varies by model.

parts.text: Existing research often treats seeking clarification as an alignment behavior of agents but has not explored its safety implications. When an agent requests clarification from the user due to task ambiguity, it introduces an interaction channel different from tool outputs, which may expand the prompt injection attack surface.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: The authors construct a benchmark ASPI containing 728 task-attack pairs, create ambiguous tasks by deleting a single key slot, and compare attack success rates across different channels in the execution state versus the clarification state, while keeping the task, environment, and attack goal consistent.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Evaluating ten models, the study finds that in the clarification state, ask_user attacks raise ASR for several models, e.g., Gemini-3-Flash from 2.2% to 35.7% (Table 2); Claude-Opus-4.7 maintains about 2% ASR in both states.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The benchmark is based on synthetic ambiguity constructed through single-slot deletion and single-turn interaction, and does not cover multi-turn or semantic ambiguity; the experiments rely on the ask_user tool and only consider a single external attacker, and the tested models are limited to ten models and four AgentDojo domains.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: STAC: When Innocent Tools Form Dangerous Chains for LLM Agents
titleEn: STAC: How Seemingly Harmless Tool-Calling Chains Break LLM Agents
summary: Researchers at AWS AI Labs propose Sequential Tool Attack Chaining (STAC), a multi-turn attack framework for tool-based LLM agents: it chains together tool calls that are each harmless on their own, with the malicious intent appearing only in the final step. The framework uses an automated closed-loop pipeline to generate executable tool chains, verify them in the environment, and reverse-engineer covert multi-turn prompts that induce the agent to execute them. The researchers built 483 cases and 1,352 user-agent-environment interactions on the SHADE-Arena and Agent-SafetyBench environments, covering 10 failure modes; across 8 agents including GPT-4.1, the average final attack success rate was 91.2%, exceeding 90% for all but one model, with a prompt harmfulness rate below 2% and a refusal rate below 4%.

parts.text: Agents change the external environment through tool calls, bringing security threats beyond text generation; existing safety checks mostly evaluate single tool calls in isolation and struggle to defend against multi-turn attacks where malicious intent is diluted across multiple steps.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: Proposes the STAC framework, which generates multi-step tool chains through reasoning planning, verifies feasibility by execution in real environments, reverse-engineers seemingly harmless multi-turn prefixes, and uses a planner to adaptively induce the agent to execute the final malicious call.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Across 483 cases, the average final ASR of the 8 tested agents reaches 91.2%; prompt defenses are all insufficient under multi-round adaptive attacks, with the reasoning defense reducing GPT-4.1's ASR to 58.6% in the first round but rising to 86.7% by the final round.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The evaluation relies on same-family models as judges, and the main experiments are based on single-run point estimates; attack success rates are conditional on validated tool chains and synthetic prefixes; the real MCP tool experiments are limited in scale and sequence-level monitoring was not evaluated.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Breaking the Code: Security Assessment of AI Code Agents Through Systematic Jailbreaking Attacks
titleEn: JAWS-Bench: Researchers jailbreak code agents systematically using three workspace scenarios
summary: The researchers propose JAWS-Bench, which evaluates the jailbreak risk of code agents in three progressive scenarios: empty workspace (JAWS-0), single file (JAWS-1), and multi-file (JAWS-M), and includes a four-stage judging process that checks compliance, attack success, syntactic correctness, and executable operation in sequence. Across seven LLM backends from five families, JAWS-0, using only text prompts, has a compliance rate of 61%, of which 58% is harmful, 52% is parseable, and 27% runs end-to-end; in JAWS-1, stronger models achieve compliance rates near 100%, with an average attack success rate of about 71%; in JAWS-M, the average attack success rate is about 75%, with 32% generating runnable attack code. The authors claim that wrapping LLMs as agents increases the attack success rate by 1.6 times on average, because the planning and tool-calling stages overturn the initial refusal. Spyware, phishing, and privilege escalation tasks are the most easily weaponized. After adding safety evaluation instructions to the system prompt, most models' compliance rates drop by about 19 to 43 percentage points, while Qwen3-235B shows almost no change.

parts.text: Existing jailbreak evaluations for code LLMs mostly focus on text refusal or harmful content detection, and do not assess whether agents actually generate malicious code that compiles and runs, leaving the real harm exposure of autonomous code agents with read, write, and execution permissions unknown.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: They propose JAWS-Bench, constructing three levels of workspaces: empty (JAWS-0, 182 entries), single-file (JAWS-1, 100 items), and multi-file (JAWS-M, 180 repositories), paired with a four-stage execution-aware evaluation framework covering compliance, harmfulness, syntactic correctness, and runtime correctness.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Evaluating 7 large models across 5 families, it finds that embedding code context raises the attack success rate; after wrapping as an agent, the ASR is on average 1.6 times that of the base model; under multi-file settings, the average ASR reaches 74.06%, and 31.27% of the generated code is deployable malicious code with no runtime errors end to end.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: Experiments are limited to a Docker single-container sandbox with no network access, not covering outbound attacks; JAWS-M retains only a single masked location; defenses only evaluate system prompt safety instructions; query costs and repeated variance are not reported for some tests.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Measuring the Security of Mobile LLM Agents under Adversarial Prompts from Untrusted Third-Party Channels
titleEn: MobiRed framework evaluates prompt injection attacks via third-party channels on eight mobile LLM agents
summary: The researchers proposed the MobiRed automated evaluation framework, conducting 3,160 adversarial tests on eight mobile LLM agents on Android, examining whether content injected through third-party channels can steer agents from user tasks toward attacker goals. The attacker does not control the device, system, apps, or the agent itself, and can only deliver content through non-app-controlled channels such as in-app ads, embedded web pages, email, SMS, and cross-app notifications. Results show that all tested agents are vulnerable to at least one attack workflow: low-friction attacks such as fake interstitial ads succeeded at rates above 85%, while malware installation workflows requiring bypassing system warnings in the attack chain achieved an average attack success rate of 18.75% against advanced agents such as Mobile-Agent-E. Simplified attacks were more effective, dense UIs such as calendars lowered success rates, and models with higher benign task completion were also more exploitable in attacks; the authors therefore claim a coupling between capability and risk and call for defenses tailored to the mobile ecosystem's unique attack surface.

parts.text: Mobile LLM agents have screen perception and cross-app execution permissions, but during operation they must process third-party content not controlled by the app, such as ads and notifications. If the agent cannot isolate trust boundaries, an attacker does not need to control the device or app to manipulate it as a confused deputy, endangering system and data security.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: The authors built an automated testing framework called MobiRed. The framework uses YAML configuration to combine benign tasks with attack workflows, patterns, and distribution channels into test cases, injects inputs on an Android test bed and collects multidimensional telemetry, and finally uses an automated evaluator to quantify attack progress across three stages: Notice, Attempt, and Execute.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Executed 3,160 rounds of adversarial tests across 8 mobile agents. Low-friction scam ads were broadly effective, with fake login achieving an average execution rate of 51.25%; malware deployment requiring bypassing system warnings succeeded 9/10 times on Mobile-Agent-E; backbone models with high benign task completion rates generally exhibited higher attack execution success rates.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The paper's main text does not set up a dedicated section to discuss limitations and future directions. The experiments cover 8 mobile agent architectures and 12 backbone models, running 3,160 test rounds on Android 9–16 emulators and physical devices; they cover 8 attack workflows and in-app/cross-app channels; the study does not evaluate dedicated prompt injection defense algorithms.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Odysseus: Jailbreaking Commercial Multimodal LLM-integrated Systems via Dual Steganography
titleEn: Odysseus jailbreaks GPT-4o, Gemini-2.0, and Grok-3 with dual steganography, with attack success rates up to 99%
summary: The researchers propose Odysseus, a jailbreak paradigm targeting commercial multimodal large model integration systems, which uses dual steganography to hide both the malicious query and the model's reply in seemingly normal images. The attack proceeds in four steps: first, the malicious prompt is encoded as a binary matrix and embedded into an image using a steganographic model; after the image is sent to the target system, the system invokes an attacker-specified extraction function via function calling to decode the hidden query and generate a reply, then steganographically embeds the violating reply back into an image and returns it; the attacker decodes the content locally. Tested on GPT-4o, Gemini-2.0-pro, Gemini-2.0-flash, and Grok-3 on SafeBench and JBB-Behaviors, the average attack success rate is 78%, with a maximum of 99%, higher than the suboptimal baseline HIMRD's 57.25%. The authors state that the images generated by this method are visually indistinguishable from the original images, with SSIM 0.8361 and PSNR 68.5971, and can bypass the input filtering of the OpenAI Moderation API with a detection rate of 0%.

parts.text: The safety filters of existing commercial MLLM integration systems are based on the assumption that malicious content must explicitly appear in the input or output. When attackers exploit cross-modal interactions to hide adversarial intent, this assumption fails, leaving blind spots in existing defenses.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: Odysseus introduces a dual-steganography paradigm: first, malicious text is encoded into a binary matrix and embedded into a carrier image; then, through function calls, the victim system is prompted to extract the prompt, generate a violating response, and re-embed it back into an image; finally, the attacker decodes and extracts the response locally.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: On GPT-4o, Gemini-2.0-pro, Gemini-2.0-flash, and Grok-3, Odysseus achieves an average ASR of 78% across two benchmarks, with Grok-3 reaching 99% on JBB-Behaviors, and fully bypasses the OpenAI review API.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: Method evaluation covers only 4 commercial closed-source MLLM systems and 2 benchmarks; Hamming codes support only single-bit error correction, and character-level recovery accuracy declines under successive transformations; and it relies heavily on function-call-based automated extraction and re-steganography mechanisms.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: DREAM: Dynamic Red-teaming across Environments for AI Models
titleEn: DREAM framework evaluates 12 LLM agents with cross-environment long-chain attacks, with over 68% of attacks bypassing existing defenses
summary: Researchers from Nanjing University, the University of Hong Kong, and other institutions propose DREAM, a framework that evaluates the interaction-level safety of LLM agents through dynamic multi-round adversarial simulation. Its core components are the cross-environment adversarial knowledge graph (CE-AKG) and context-guided policy search (C-GPS), which treat existing single-round static attacks as atomic actions and assemble them into long-chain attack trajectories across environments. Based on an atomic attack library of 1,986 attacks built from 349 digital environments, the researchers evaluated 12 SOTA agents and found that over 68% of long-chain attacks successfully bypassed existing defenses, with 8 models having attack success rates above 70%. The severity of vulnerabilities exposed by 5-step attack chains across 5 environments was 4.8 times that of the static baseline. Claude-Sonnet-4.5 had the lowest average attack success rate (48.31%), but once a long-chain attack succeeded, its severity score (14.4) was the highest among all models.

parts.text: Existing multi-agent safety evaluations are limited to static single-turn tests and cannot capture long-chain attack threats that accumulate from seemingly benign operations across multiple environments and multi-turn interactions.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: DREAM models attacks as a partially observable Markov decision process, dynamically combining atomic attacks and backtracking planning based on a cross-environment adversarial knowledge graph and context-guided policy search.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Evaluation of 12 models found that over 68% of long-chain attacks bypassed defenses; Claude-Sonnet-4.5 achieved the highest overall defense score of 67.30, but its harm score reached 14.4 after long-chain breakthroughs.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The evaluation covers 12 models and 349 environments; the 5-environment path sample is relatively small; reliance on closed-source APIs affects full reproducibility; high-privilege local agents such as OpenClaw are not yet covered.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

titleEn: MultiTurnPSB: Four-round medical jailbreak evaluation shows single-round benchmarks mask a 19x safety gap
summary: The researchers propose MultiTurnPSB, extending the 466 patient-facing medical safety prompts from PatientSafetyBench into four-turn adversarial dialogues, and test three attack methods: fixed template, template adaptive, and live adversarial. Under live adversarial attack, GPT-4.1-mini's unsafe response rate rose from 34.8% at Turn 1 to 78.8% at Turn 4, with health misinformation rising from 15.0% to 83.8% and discrimination reaching 89.0%. Against the same GPT-4o-mini attacker, GPT-4.1-mini and Claude Sonnet 4.5 were nearly indistinguishable at Turn 1 (34.8% vs. 31.8%, p=0.43), but by Turn 4 there was a 19-fold gap (78.8% vs. 4.1%). The authors identified four degradation trajectories and noted that the two-element combination of emergency framing plus medical authority claims was associated with most complete violations, with Turn 2 being a key vulnerability window.

parts.text: When faced with a refusal, patients often add urgency and authority pressure; existing benchmarks only test a single turn and cannot reflect the medical safety risks in real conversations.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: Build a four-round, three-modality adversarial benchmark MultiTurnPSB based on PSB, and test the effect of input-side label intervention by six classifiers.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: GPT-4.1-mini's unsafe rate rose to 78.8% under real-time attack; input-side label intervention reduced it by 52.2 percentage points but had a 45.0% false positive rate.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The benchmark is English-only and text-only, the tested models were not configured with system prompts, and Claude as the attacker is contaminated by refusals in the last two turns.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Do Coding Agents Understand Least-Privilege Authorization?
titleEn: The paper proposes the AuthBench benchmark to evaluate whether coding agents can infer minimal permission boundaries.
summary: The paper defines the ability of a coding Agent to generate file-level read/write/execute permission policies before task execution as permission boundary inference, and constructs the AuthBench benchmark, containing 120 terminal tasks across 10 domains (80 standard tasks, 40 sensitive tasks), with human-reviewed permission annotations and executable utility and attack verifiers. Evaluating frontier models including GPT-5, GPT-5.3-Codex, GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, Kimi K2.5, MiniMax M2.7, Qwen3-Coder-480B, Qwen3.5-397B, the study finds that models frequently exhibit both under-granting and over-granting: they omit permissions required by the execution chain while also granting unused or sensitive access. Increasing inference-time compute does not narrow this gap; instead, it makes each model converge more stably to its own authorization attractor.

parts.text: Code agents lack a mechanism for granting least privilege on demand before executing terminal tasks, and coarse-grained default permissions easily introduce security risks; existing research assumes permission policies are given and does not study whether agents can autonomously infer task-level permission boundaries before acting.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: Proposes a two-stage Sufficiency-Tightness Decomposition: Phase 1 forward-simulates the execution plan and parses the complete toolchain to generate a permissive policy with coverage first; Phase 2 performs item-by-item audit filtering based on task rationale, scope minimization, and sensitive surfaces.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: On AuthBench, frontier models often both under- and over-authorize; increasing reasoning instead makes models converge to their own preferred authorization attractors. The two-stage decomposition improves the TSR of tightness-biased models on sensitive tasks by up to 15.8%, and reduces the attack success rate on all tested models.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The paper's limitations are that the policy language only covers file-level read/write/execute permissions in terminal tasks, not network access, IPC, database credentials, cloud resources, browser state, or API-level permissions; reasoning intensity analysis is limited to model families with configurable reasoning levels. The evaluation covers 120 terminal tasks and 9 frontier models, and does not report other non-file-system permissions.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: CORVUS: Red-Teaming Hallucination Detectors via Internal Signal Camouflage in Large Language Models
titleEn: CORVUS: Using LoRA to disguise internal signals and bypass single-forward hallucination detectors
summary: Researchers from Singapore Management University and other institutions propose CORVUS, a white-box model-side red-teaming method: freezing the detector and base model, using only a LoRA adapter under teacher forcing to reshape three types of internal telemetry signals in the answer window—token entropy (TE), hidden-state log-volume (HV), and attention diagonality (AD)—and adding a one-step embedding-space FGSM attention stress test. The adapter is trained on only 1,000 out-of-distribution Alpaca instructions with fewer than 0.5% trainable parameters, then transfers zero-shot to FAVA-Annotation, simultaneously weakening both training-free detectors (e.g., LLM-Check) and probe-based detectors (SEP, ICR-probe) across four open-source models: Llama-2, Vicuna, Llama-3, and Qwen2.5. Ablations show that the AD term is the main lever for evading attention-based features, with TE and HV providing secondary shaping.

parts.text: Single-pass hallucination detectors rely on the model's internal computational telemetry (such as uncertainty, hidden state geometry, and attention). Previous evaluations assumed the model is passive and did not consider the risk that, in open-weight or self-hosted deployments, a model-side adversary could evade detection by modifying the model's internal representations.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: The authors propose the CORVUS method, which freezes the base model and trains a lightweight LoRA adapter. Under teacher forcing, it directly optimizes the token entropy and hidden log-volume of the answer tokens, and introduces an adversarial attention diagonality loss via single-step embedding-space FGSM perturbation, camouflaging internal telemetry while keeping the surface answer unchanged.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: The adapter is trained on 1,000 Alpaca instructions and then zero-shot transferred to FAVA-Annotation. The authors report that it reduces the performance of training-free detectors and probes on Llama-2, Vicuna, Llama-3, and Qwen2.5, with attention score AUROC dropping to 48.08 on Llama-2.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The method assumes white-box access and is not directly applicable to closed-source APIs; experiments are limited to single-forward internal detectors; the method only camouflages internal signals without optimizing factuality, so it cannot fix hallucinations themselves; the paper does not report defense effectiveness against external detectors such as retrieval-augmented ones.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: When Autoregressive Consistency Hurts Safety Alignment
titleEn: The paper proposes a random insertion attack that exploits autoregressive consistency to bypass LLM safety alignment
summary: The paper "When Autoregressive Consistency Hurts Safety Alignment" proposes that the safety alignment of large language models is fragile partly because it is often shallow: fine-tuning mainly changes the model's behavior near the first few output tokens. The authors explain this phenomenon with autoregressive consistency, i.e., next-token prediction tends to maintain and continue the current response trajectory, and learning dynamics analysis shows that alignment updates concentrate on early tokens. The same mechanism also predicts a broader class of attacks, namely inducing harmful continuation states at arbitrary positions in the output trajectory. As a concrete example, the authors propose a random insertion attack, which inserts a short harmful segment into an otherwise safe refusal trajectory, leveraging autoregressive consistency to maintain the harmful branch and thereby bypass safety alignment; even after a very long refusal prefix, a short harmful segment can steer generation toward harm. Based on this, the authors propose an adversarial safety alignment framework, instantiated as random worst-insertion training, and argue that safety alignment should break harmful autoregressive consistency across the entire output trajectory.

parts.text: Safety alignment is meant to make the model refuse harmful queries, but fine-tuning often changes only the first few output tokens, and the model may remain vulnerable after the refusal prefix. The authors argue this is related to autoregressive consistency.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: Analyzing the learning dynamics, they state that autoregressive consistency concentrates alignment updates on early tokens. The attack example, random insertion attack, inserts a short harmful span into a refusal trajectory. Alignment instead uses worst-case harmful continuation states, with the initial implementation called random worst-insertion attack.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: The authors state that autoregressive consistency causes alignment updates to concentrate on early tokens. The authors also state that a short harmful segment, even when placed after a very long refusal prefix, can still steer generation toward harm.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The abstract does not describe something as a limitation. The authors refer to the alignment implementation as a preliminary random worst-insertion attack and argue that alignment should also break harmful autoregressive consistency throughout the entire output.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Visual Exclusivity Attacks: Automatic Multimodal Red Teaming via Agentic Planning
titleEn: The researchers propose the MM-Plan multimodal jailbreak framework, with an attack success rate of 46.3% against Claude 4.5 Sonnet
summary: The researchers propose the Visual Exclusivity (VE) threat model and the MM-Plan multimodal multi-turn agent planning framework, shifting jailbreaks from per-turn reactions to global strategy synthesis. The attacker planner is trained with GRPO and can discover effective strategies on its own without human supervision. On the VE-Safety dataset constructed by the authors, MM-Plan achieves an attack success rate of 46.3% against Claude 4.5 Sonnet and 13.8% against GPT-5; the authors state it outperforms baselines by 2 to 5 times, while existing methods mostly fail. The authors believe this result shows that frontier models remain vulnerable to agentic multimodal attacks, and there is a gap in current safety alignment.

parts.text: Existing multimodal red teaming mostly treats images as containers for malicious text. Once the payload can be recovered by OCR or description, text-side alignment can block it. What the authors address is: the harm comes only from the spatial and functional relations in technical images, text alone is insufficient, and it often takes multiple turns to complete.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: MM-Plan uses Qwen3-VL-4B to write persona, narrative, and crop/mask/blur in one pass. After execution, a reviewer model scores, then GRPO updates. VE-Safety has 440 human instances; neither text nor 512-token descriptions are sufficient to complete the goal.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: On the VE-Safety test set, MM-Plan's ASR is 46.3% against Claude 4.5 Sonnet, 13.8% against GPT-5, and 65.0% against InternVL3-8B (Table 3). GPT-5's second highest is Crescendo at 3.1%.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The paper does not have a dedicated section discussing limitations. Experiments include 8 MLLMs, 320 items in the VE-Safety test, and 30 items in the HarmBench filtered test. 400 items were manually verified. The main ASR judge model, Claude 4.5 Sonnet, is also the target under test.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: DECEIVE-AFC: Adversarial Claim Attacks against Search-Enabled LLM-based Fact-Checking Systems
titleEn: DECEIVE-AFC: Adversarial Claim Attacks against Retrieval-Augmented LLM Fact-Checking Systems
summary: The researchers propose DECEIVE-AFC, an agentic adversarial attack framework against retrieval-based LLM fact-checking systems, operating under a threat model where only the input claim can be modified, without relying on access to evidence sources or model internals. The framework combines claim-level attack strategies with principles for evaluating the effectiveness of adversarial claims, systematically searching for attack trajectories that interfere with search behavior, evidence retrieval, and LLM reasoning. Evaluations on benchmark datasets and real systems show that the attack reduces fact-checking accuracy from 78.7% to 53.7%, significantly outperforms existing claim-based attack baselines, and exhibits strong cross-system transferability.

parts.text: Search-enhanced LLM fact-checking dynamically retrieves open web evidence. Existing adversarial claim attacks mostly target static corpora or character-level perturbations, and when only the input claim can be modified, they struggle to cause system-level fact-checking failures.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: DECEIVE-AFC uses an agent closed loop to rewrite claims, influencing queries, retrieval, and reasoning through search engine misguidance, reasoning disruption, and structural complexity escalation, and constrains factual intent with similarity, NLI, and reasoning relevance; it iterates on the surrogate system before transfer.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: On filtered MOCHEG, DEFAME accuracy drops from 78.7% to 53.7%, with ASR of 31.4%; HiSS and LEMMA have ASR of 19.5% and 18.8%, higher than the character-level baselines in the same table. The surrogate model itself has ASR of 36.6%.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The paper does not specifically discuss limitations. The Discussion proposes fine-tuning the fact-checking model and adversarial-aware validation in the interpretation and retrieval stages. Experiments cover HiSS, LEMMA, DEFAME, and the filtered 1642 items; the sample size for human confirmation and per-strategy ASR are not reported.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Adversarial Bug Reports as a Security Risk in Language Model-Based Automated Program Repair
titleEn: Study: adversarial bug reports can induce LLM automated program repair systems to generate unsafe patches
summary: The researchers propose and validate a new attack surface against LLM-based automated program repair (APR) systems: adversarial bug reports, i.e., issue submissions that appear realistic but are designed to induce the system to produce insecure or harmful code. The team built a threat model and generated 51 adversarial bug reports, covering strategies from manual to fully automated pipelines, and tested them on a mainstream LLM APR system. Results show that 90% of the constructed reports triggered patches consistent with the attacker's intent; the best-performing pre-repair filter only blocked 47%, and post-repair detection (GitHub Copilot, CodeQL, often requiring human intervention) was effective in only 58% of cases. The authors also released a prototype framework for automatically generating adversarial bug reports, and pointed out a structural asymmetry where generating attack inputs is low-cost, while detection and mitigation are costly and error-prone.

parts.text: LLM-based APR automatically modifies code based on natural language bug reports and may submit patches. The authors state that public issues receive little review, and an adversary can submit realistic-looking reports, causing the system to write insecure changes, leak secrets in CI, or waste compute. They state that this input channel has not been systematically studied.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: The authors use DevStral:24B to generate five categories of bug reports: irrelevant synthesis, deceptive noise, CI/CD exploitation, vulnerability injection, and reverting CVE fixes. The latter three use LSH and fuzzy matching to extract and clean commit context. They then evaluate pre-filtering, project tests, CodeQL, and Copilot on SWE-agent.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: All 51 generated patches, 46 matched the attack objective. Testing showed 35/51 with no new failures. Plain-text o4-mini detected 24/51, CodeQL detected 0, and Copilot security alerts covered 30/51. Total generation cost was $0.0133, with an APR average of $0.87 per item.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors point out extrapolation, annotation subjectivity, and failure to set temperature to 0. The experiment is a summary of 51 items from SWE-agent and five SWE-bench projects; the paper does not report project distribution, number of repetitions, or annotation consistency.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: When Child Inherits: Modeling and Exploiting Subagent Spawn in Multi-Agent Networks
titleEn: The paper models the sub-agent inheritance attack surface in multi-agent networks
summary: The paper proposes modeling multi-agent networks from the perspective of sub-agent inheritance, pointing out that a parent agent's memory can carry malicious instructions, stale state, or unexpected behavior rules into newly created sub-agents, allowing local compromise to spread across agent boundaries. The authors claim that current frameworks violate trust boundaries in areas such as insecure memory inheritance, weak resource control, stale state after derivation, and improper termination permissions, and they demonstrate these risks in real agent frameworks. They then propose a defense based on explicit security invariants. The research argues that inheritance is not just an implementation detail but a core component affecting multi-agent system security.

parts.text: Multi-agent frameworks inherit parent memory when generating sub-agents and delegate resources and termination rights. The authors argue that a compromised agent can therefore pass malicious instructions and stale state across trust boundaries.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: The authors formalize role-based multi-agent networks in terms of hierarchy, capabilities, memory patterns, and interaction patterns, and give three invariants: termination scope, memory isolation, and resource access. The defenses are an immutable-after-generation capability registry, role-projected memory, and an append-only revision log.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: The four PoC categories on OpenClaw 3.13 were made into expired verification commits, unauthorized self-start, sub-agents inheriting parent rules, and sibling termination. Table III shows all five models reproduced them. Agent Zero and Hermes only have task-oriented sub-agents, so cross-mode termination does not occur by construction.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors state that the formal model does not include execution semantics and does not cover non-role-based or identity-based access control; future work will use reasoning within deterministic boundaries and adapt defenses to different scenarios. The experiments are a qualitative PoC on OpenClaw 3.13 plus Table III with five models; the paper does not report success rates, number of repetitions, or the LLM used for the main PoC.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Exposing LLM Safety Gaps Through Mathematical Encoding:New Attacks and Systematic Analysis
titleEn: The study uses mathematical encoding to bypass LLM safety filters, with an average attack success rate of 46%–56% across eight models
summary: The researchers propose rewriting harmful prompts into coherent mathematical problems such as set theory, formal logic, and quantum mechanics, which can bypass LLM safety filters at a high rate, with an average attack success rate of 46%–56% across eight target models and two existing benchmarks. The authors point out that the effectiveness of the attack does not depend on the mathematical symbols themselves, but on whether a helper LLM deeply rewrites the harmful content into genuine mathematical problems; rule-based encodings that only apply mathematical formatting perform similarly to the unencoded baseline. The study also proposes a new formal logic encoding with an attack success rate comparable to set theory, showing the vulnerability generalizes across different mathematical forms; repetition post-processing experiments also show the attack remains robust to simple prompt enhancements. Newer GPT-5 and GPT-5-Mini are notably more robust than older models, but still vulnerable. The authors accordingly argue that current safety frameworks have a structural gap requiring defenses that reason about mathematical structure rather than surface semantics.

parts.text: Safety mechanisms mainly match harmful intent in natural language. The authors ask whether filters still identify harmful content after encoding it as set theory, formal logic, or quantum mechanics problems; and they separate deep rewriting from merely adding mathematical formatting.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: Under black-box, a helper (GPT-4.1-Mini) or deterministic rules encode harmful prompts into six mathematical forms, then submit them with problem-solving or decoding instructions. GPT-5-Nano makes binary judgments according to the HarmBench protocol. Repeated experiments concatenate the encoded results verbatim once more.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: On HarmBench (159 items) and JailbreakBench (100 items), the authors report average ASR for eight-model LLM encoding as 46.3% and 55.9%, and for four-model rule-based encoding as 11.0% and 8.8%. The average ∆ASR across 56 repetitions is −0.46%.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors note: only GPT-5-Nano automatic evaluation, no human evaluation; binary ASR does not distinguish executability; the two encoding types are also confounded by length, complexity, and format; experiments are in English and ASR is not broken down by harm category; API versions are opaque; repetition is only verbatim copying. ISM was not tested. Rule-based encodings and repetition cover only four models.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Judge Reliability Harness: Stress Testing the Reliability of LLM Judges
titleEn: Researchers release Judge Reliability Harness, stress-testing LLM judge reliability
summary: The researchers release the open-source library Judge Reliability Harness for building validation suites to test the reliability of LLM judges. The tool generates reliability tests for a given benchmark dataset and judge configuration, evaluating binary judgment accuracy and ordinal scoring performance, covering free-form and agent task formats. The authors evaluate four frontier judges on four benchmarks covering safety, persuasion, abuse, and agent behavior, finding notable differences across models and perturbation types, with no judge consistently reliable across all benchmarks. Preliminary experiments show that simple text format changes, paraphrasing, verbosity changes, and flipping true labels in LLM answers affect the accuracy with which judges assess another model's task completion ability. The code is open-sourced, and the paper is accepted at the ICLR 2026 Agents in the Wild workshop.

parts.text: LLMs are used as judges or autograders in evaluations, but model, rubric, and prompt configurations are rarely measured systematically. Agreement with humans on a small validation set does not reveal performance under changes in format, rewriting, verbosity, or sampling parameters.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: Given a benchmark and judge configuration, JRH generates label-flip, formatting, paraphrase, length, duplicate, ordinal-bucket, and agent transcript variants, optionally with human acceptance or modification, then computes the proportion of judge scores matching the target label.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Four judges are not equally stable across four benchmarks. The authors state that no judge is stable across all benchmarks, Persuade is more fragile than binary-classification benchmarks, and cross-judge means are lower on format tests except for Fortress. The authors state that Llama 4.1 Maverick 17B tends to be more stable, at a fraction of the cost of other judges.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The paper does not list limitations. It covers four judges and four benchmarks; the first three benchmarks have 10 items each, and AgentHarm has 16. It does not report confidence intervals, agreement with humans, or ordinal generation temperature.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: ContextLeak: Auditing Leakage in Private In-Context Learning Methods
titleEn: ContextLeak: Auditing Privacy Leakage in Private In-Context Learning
summary: The researchers propose ContextLeak, a framework for empirically measuring worst-case information leakage in in-context learning (ICL). The method uses canary insertion to embed uniquely identifiable tokens into sensitive datasets, and constructs targeted queries to detect whether they appear. The authors apply it to various private ICL techniques, including heuristic prompt defenses and differentially private methods with formal guarantees, and the results show that ContextLeak can reliably detect leakage in each method, and that leakage increases monotonically with the theoretical privacy budget. The analysis also shows that existing methods trade off poorly between privacy and utility, either fully leaking sensitive information or severely harming performance.

parts.text: ICL puts examples that may contain sensitive information into the prompt, and malicious users may still extract information from the output. Heuristic defenses provide no privacy guarantees against an adversary, and DP upper bounds may be too loose, lacking an audit of measured worst-case leakage.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: ContextLeak inserts an identifiable canary into the sensitive context with probability 0.5, and submits adversarial queries, judging whether the canary exists only based on the privatized output, thereby giving an empirical ε lower bound. The query templates can be further optimized with GEPA.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Audit RNM, ESA, and L0–L3 on Llama3.3-70b, Qwen2.5-72b, and GPT-4.1. The authors state that leakage increases with theoretical ε; prompt injection achieves near 50% audit accuracy on L3, while this audit shows full leakage. RNM utility stagnates after empirical ε of about 0.4.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors note that only single-round queries are evaluated, synthetic-data-type DP is not systematically covered, and the canary and query designs are not exhaustive. The main experimental models are three large models, with an additional three small models for ablation; the DP audit uses aggregated outputs rather than final outputs.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Jailbreak-AudioBench: In-Depth Evaluation and Analysis of Jailbreak Threats for Large Audio Language Models
titleEn: Jailbreak-AudioBench: A Jailbreak Evaluation Benchmark for Large Audio Language Models
summary: The researchers propose Jailbreak-AudioBench for systematically evaluating audio jailbreak threats to large audio language models (LALMs), comprising a toolbox, a curated dataset, and a benchmark. The toolbox supports text-to-audio and multiple editing techniques that inject hidden semantics into audio. The dataset provides explicit and implicit jailbreak audio samples in both original and edited forms. The authors evaluate several current advanced LALMs with this dataset, claim it establishes the most comprehensive audio-modality jailbreak benchmark to date, and hope to expose stronger jailbreak threats such as query-based audio editing, advancing LALM safety alignment and defense research.

parts.text: End-to-end LALMs directly perceive hidden semantics such as speaking rate, pitch, noise, accent, and emotion. The authors say text and visual jailbreak research is abundant, but audio jailbreak still lacks systematic evaluation, and such edits may bypass safety constraints.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: Use gTTS to convert jailbreak text to audio, then apply edits for volume, speed, intonation, pitch, noise, accent, and emotion. Questions are divided into Explicit and Implicit; ASR requires Llama Guard 3 to judge harmful and exceed 50 words. Also query with 32 combinations, and prepend audio instructions that refuse harmful content to the samples.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: After editing, ASR relative to the original audio goes up and down. On Explicit Small, query-based composition raises SALMONN-7B's ASR from 31.6% to 85.1%, and Gemini-2.5-Flash from 8.1% to 49.4%. The authors state that prepended audio instructions lower ASR, but the remaining values are still high.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors note that Llama Guard 3 misclassifies repetition as success, and plan to change the metric and add natural speech. The evaluation covers 10 end-to-end models, one inference per sample; the closed-source main table uses small sets of 262/237 samples, and Figure 6/9 do not include these two closed-source models.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: Easier to Mislead Than to Correct: Harmful and Beneficial Revision in LLM Conformity
titleEn: Study: LLMs in multi-agent systems are more easily misled by peer consensus than corrected by it
summary: The paper conducts a controlled study of conformity behavior in LLMs within multi-agent systems: the model answers a question, then sees simulated peer answers and gives a final answer, manipulating two social cues: consensus structure and peer authority labels. Across four open-weight models and seven QA datasets, unanimous peer agreement misleads originally correct models at a much higher rate than it corrects originally wrong answers; authority labels make models more likely to choose the endorsed answer, regardless of its correctness. The authors also find that general reasoning interventions like chain-of-thought and reflection cannot reliably reduce harmful revisions while preserving beneficial ones, and therefore recommend that multi-agent LLM systems should verify peer answers rather than simply aggregate them.

parts.text: In multi-agent settings, a model may abandon its own answer because peer answers agree. The authors aim to compare, in the same controlled setting, whether this influence corrects initial errors as strongly as it misleads initially correct ones.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: The model first answers multiple-choice questions independently, then re-answers after seeing six simulated peers. Cross consensus structure with authority labels, using mixed peers as the shared baseline for both types of revision, and additionally test CoT and reflect-then-revise.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Without authority, when aggregating four models, the harmful revision rate under all-wrong is 62.9% (mixed 15.6%), and the beneficial revision rate under all-correct is 51.5% (mixed 32.7%, Table 1). As the number of authoritative figures increases, revisions more often move toward the endorsed option, regardless of correctness. Neither of the two reasoning prompts can suppress only harmful revisions.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors note the limitations of using only multiple-choice questions and simulated peers rather than live conversations, and that self-rated confidence is not a calibrated probability; they plan to continue with live multi-agent settings and open-ended generation. The experiments use four open-source models, 2,500 multiple-choice questions, and three seeds, with correctness judged against the gold label.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: RedDiffuser: Auditing Multimodal Safety Failures in Vision-Language Models via Reinforced Diffusion
titleEn: RedDiffuser: Using reinforcement diffusion to generate visual inputs for auditing VLM multimodal safety failures
summary: The researchers propose RedDiffuser (RedDiff), a reinforcement-based framework that uses diffusion models to generate semantically coherent visual inputs for black-box safety testing, combining greedy prompt search with reinforcement optimization to mine high-risk multimodal inputs that expose potential safety failures in VLMs. The paper studies multimodal safety auditing under exposure to harmful contexts, i.e., whether VLMs can maintain safe behavior when partially harmful text is paired with visual contexts. Experiments on open-source and commercial VLMs show that failures under such contextual conditions are relatively common: on LLaVA, RedDiffuser increases the unsafe response rate by up to 10.69% on the original set and 8.91% on the held-out set, and transfers to Gemini and LLaMA-Vision. The authors state that these vulnerabilities persist under external safety guardrails, indicating that current system-level safety mechanisms are still insufficient for real-world multimodal risks.

parts.text: VLMs in open environments often face incomplete, ambiguous multimodal inputs. The authors argue that testing only explicit malicious instructions misses a risk: when partially toxic text is paired with visual context, can safety alignment still block harmful continuations.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: RedDiffuser: with text fixed, Gemini greedily searches image prompts, then DDPO fine-tunes the diffusion model. The reward is Detoxify toxicity score plus λ times BERTScore. The guardrail variant zeroes the toxicity reward for samples that fail the dual NSFW check.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: LLaVA main subset Detoxify Any*: text-only 58.01%, aligned (M) 68.70% (Table 1). Hold-out unaligned variant 79.45% (Table 2). On Gemini-1.5-flash, aligned (M) 81.33% (Table 3).
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The paper does not specifically discuss limitations. The target model is LLaVA-1.5-7B, and it is transferred to Gemini-1.5-flash and LLaMA-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct. The paper does not report the number of repetitions or human agreement.

title: Memento 3: Model-Based Recursive Self-Improvement through Reflective Rulebooks
titleEn: Memento 3 proposes a rulebook-based recursive self-improvement method
summary: The paper proposes Memento 3, enabling frozen large language model agents to continuously learn an explicit world model through external memory. The agent maintains a natural language rulebook as persistent semantic memory, recording revisable hypotheses about environment dynamics, and compiles the rulebook into executable code for prediction and planning. Through a continuous loop of observation, reflection, rule revision, compilation, and verification, the agent uses prediction errors to improve both the rulebook and the code; updated code is accepted only when the LLM judges that the code faithfully reflects the rulebook and that cell-by-cell replay reproduces the observed state transitions. The authors view this process as a model-based path toward recursive self-improvement, with the underlying LLM kept fixed. A population-scale extension maintains multiple world models in parallel, sharing interaction evidence and using its predictions to guide exploration.

parts.text: With limited interaction, multiple world models can fit at the same time, yet they differ in predictions on unseen states. A frozen-parameter LLM still needs to revise explicit environment rules in order to plan in unfamiliar environments.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: Code as Model treats the natural language rulebook as semantic memory and compiles it into executable code for prediction and planning. Prediction errors drive reflection, revision, compilation, and verification; accepting updates requires that the code be faithful to the rulebook and that replay reproduce observed transitions cell by cell. Multiple models can be maintained in parallel and share evidence.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: On 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, the single-model setting completes all, with average RHAE of 100.0 and total actions at 0.44 of the human count. On Pong, the learned controller wins 21:0 across three different starting positions, with no further LLM calls at execution time.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The paper does not specifically discuss limitations. The report covers single-model results on 25 public games, rulebook ablations on three games, and an N=2 population on wa30; the Pong controller is evaluated on three openings. The paper does not report the number of main experiment repetitions or the number of LLM calls for ARC-AGI-3 learning.
parts.label: Limitations and future work

title: You Changed Your Mind, The Model Didn't: Demystifying Intent in Multi-Turn Dialogue
titleEn: The paper proposes the Intent-Eval benchmark, revealing that models confuse rejected intents in multi-turn dialogue
summary: The paper finds that large language models in multi-turn tasks treat proposals the user has rejected or replaced as still-active requirements; even when the user's final intent is unchanged, task execution can be led astray. The authors propose Intent-Eval, a controlled benchmark covering tool operation, code, database, and math tasks. Models are fragile on both rejected proposals and replaced requirements, and accuracy drops deepen or persist as interaction continues. To address this, the authors propose Intent-OPSD, an on-policy self-distillation framework under decision conditions. Teacher and Student are initialized from the same model; the frozen Teacher provides active-intent supervision based on the complete task matched to the user's decisions, and the Student is trained to follow the active requirements reflecting user intent over the full dialogue.

parts.text: In multi-turn tasks, after the user proposes a change and then rejects or revises it, the model may still answer according to content that was mentioned. The authors argue that what was said needs to be distinguished from requirements still in effect; otherwise task execution can be led astray.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: Intent-Eval turns the same source task into four multi-turn conditions: no insertion, clarification only, refused proposal, accepted proposal, with single-turn controls. Intent-OPSD's frozen teacher sees the full single-turn task matching the decision, and the student performs on-policy self-distillation on the full conversation with token-level JS divergence.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Across eight models, multi-turn Original drops 36.30 percentage points from single-turn, and Retained and Revised drop another 8.06 and 5.55 percentage points. Across ten models, 59.63% of new Retained errors contain invalidated content. Intent-OPSD is 10.81 percentage points higher than Base across four models.
parts.label: Experiments and results

title: APEXA: Execution-Integrity Enforcement for Multi-Agent LLM Automation of Synchrotron Data Reduction
titleEn: APEXA adds execution integrity guardrails to LLM multi-agent systems for synchrotron data processing
summary: The paper proposes APEXA, a deployed framework that coordinates 61 tools for synchrotron data reduction and, through deterministic execution integrity guardrails, prevents returning results for tool calls that were not actually executed. The same tool layer also enforces motor safety constraints: over 50 adversarial scenarios and four models, it produced 0/200 violations against a simulated EPICS controller, versus 15/200 for the prompt-only baseline. The authors also release APEXA-Bench, containing 58 facility tasks organized by scientific correctness and physical consequence; on real APS beamline data, a single prompt recovered detector geometry and integrated a complete attenuation and exposure scan. The authors argue that trustworthy scientific agents require deterministic execution verification rather than model-side guarantees, and they release the framework, benchmark, and trajectories.

parts.text: Synchrotron data reduction is a multi-step expert process, and a language model's fluent reply does not mean the requested computation has been executed. Institutional gateways may also silently drop tool calls, and the model may still narrate calibrations that were not run.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: APEXA uses one reasoning agent to call 61 tools. A deterministic tool layer refuses to return results without an execution record and runs five checks before motor commands are issued. APEXA-BENCH contains 58 tasks labeled by four types of physical consequence.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: On 50 adversarial scenarios, four models, and a simulated EPICS IOC, tool-layer violations are 0/200, and the prompt-only baseline with roughly 700 tokens is 15/200. On APS 1-ID, one prompt completes calibration and integration, the detector distance in a CeO2 decay scan stays within ±0.02 mm, and non-physical calibrations are rejected.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The paper does not specifically discuss limitations. This paper reports motor safety gates and cross-detector task completion; large-scale scoring is left to the full paper, and the main text has no APEXA-Score. §IV-C only evaluates task completion, not refinement accuracy.

title: Echoes of Human Malice in Agents: Benchmarking LLMs for Multi-Turn Online Harassment Attacks
titleEn: The paper proposes a multi-turn online harassment agent benchmark; jailbreak fine-tuning raises the attack success rate above 95%
summary: The paper proposes the Online Harassment Agentic Benchmark, using a synthetic multi-turn harassment dialogue dataset, a multi-agent (harasser, victim) simulation based on repeated game theory, three jailbreak methods targeting memory/planning/fine-tuning, and a hybrid evaluation framework, to test two models: LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and Gemini-2.0-flash. Results show that jailbreak fine-tuning makes harassment almost inevitable, with attack success rate on Llama rising from 57.25–64.19% to 95.78–96.89%, on Gemini from 98.46% to 99.33%, and refusal rates for both models dropping to 1–2%. The most common harmful behaviors are insults (84.9–87.8%, 44.2–50.8% without fine-tuning) and aggressive flaming (81.2–85.1%, 31.5–38.8% without fine-tuning), indicating that guardrails for these behaviors are weaker than for sensitive categories such as sexual harassment or racial harassment.

parts.text: Online harassment often escalates over multiple turns, while existing jailbreak evaluations mostly look at single-turn prompts. Once LLM agents have long-horizon interaction, tool use, and memory, guardrail failures may amplify harassment at higher speed and persistence. The authors evaluate how memory, planning, and fine-tuning affect this kind of abuse.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: The benchmark uses Dolphin3 to expand social media seeds into multi-turn harassment conversations, then simulates a harasser and an avoidant victim with repeated games, up to 10 turns. Attacks compare persona prompting, memory injection, CoT/ReAct, and jailbreak fine-tuning. gpt-4o-mini labels by eight categories, and humans code by dark triad and conflict avoidance.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: LLaMA fine-tuned ASR 95.78–96.89%, without fine-tuning 57.25–64.19%. Qwen3 without fine-tuning 92.50–99.12%. Gemini memory 99.54%, DeepSeek-FT baseline 64.15%. The authors state that Insult and Flaming are the most common.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors note that seed data duplication accounts for 0.83% of the synthetic set, that quality evaluation did not directly use real dialogues, and plan deduplication and additional quality checks. The evaluation covers four model families, at most 10 turns, and human coding for LLaMA-FT and Gemini-FT; the main ASR table does not report the number of dialogues.

title: MEEA: Mere Exposure Effect-Driven Confrontational Optimization for LLM Jailbreaking
titleEn: MEEA: A Multi-Turn Jailbreak Attack Framework Based on the Mere Exposure Effect
summary: The researchers propose MEEA (Mere Exposure Effect Attack), a fully automated black-box multi-turn jailbreak framework inspired by the psychological mere exposure effect, which gradually erodes a model's safety alignment constraints through repeated exposure to low-toxicity semantics. The method constructs a semantically progressive prompt chain and uses a simulated annealing strategy combined with semantic similarity, toxicity, and jailbreak effectiveness for optimization. On closed-source and open-source models such as GPT-4, Claude-3.5, and DeepSeek-R1, MEEA consistently achieves higher attack success rates than seven representative baselines, with an average improvement of over 20%. Ablation experiments verify the necessity of annealing optimization and the contextual exposure mechanism. Based on this, the authors argue that LLM safety behavior is dynamic and history-dependent, challenging the assumption of static alignment boundaries, and call for interaction-aware safety evaluation and defense mechanisms.

parts.text: In multi-turn dialogue, the model's effective safety boundary shifts with context, and most jailbreaks are still designed around a static boundary, limiting stability and automation.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: MEEA generates semantically progressive multi-turn prompt chains, uses jailbreak score, toxicity, and semantic similarity as the energy function, accepts suboptimal perturbations via simulated annealing, and rolls back refusals and dead ends.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: On 50 items each from AdvBench and JailbreakBench, the MEEA ASR for five targets is higher than the seven baselines in Table 1, averaging 92.63%; without multi-turn, LLaMA-3.1-8B and GPT-4 are 51.45% and 53.26%.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors state that they only study output-layer failures in text dialogue, that external evaluation may introduce noise, and that the dynamic threshold is heuristic. The experiments do not report the attack model or hyperparameters such as N and τ.

title: How Many Iterations to Jailbreak? Dynamic Budget Allocation for Multi-Turn LLM Evaluation
titleEn: DAPRO: Dynamic budget allocation for the number of rounds needed for jailbreaks in multi-round LLM evaluation
summary: The paper proposes DAPRO (Dynamic Allocation via PRojected Optimization), a dynamic budget allocation framework for lower bounds on event occurrence times in multi-turn LLM interactions. The authors prove that the method satisfies the expected budget constraint and provides finite-sample coverage guarantees without distributional assumptions, no longer relying on the conditional independence between censoring time and event time required by previous conformal survival methods. Its coverage bound scales with the square root of the average censoring weight and involves only partial samples rather than worst-case weights, making it tighter than prior work. DAPRO can also give unbiased estimates of overall evaluation metrics such as jailbreak rate under finite compute. Across four experiment types—agent task success, LLM jailbreak, harmful content generation, and RAG hallucination—DAPRO's coverage is closer to the nominal level, has lower variance than static baselines, and does not exceed the expected budget.

parts.text: In multi-round evaluation, a successful jailbreak or an agent completing a task may take many rounds to appear, and interactive computation is expensive. The authors aim to estimate time-to-event under an expected budget and provide prediction intervals with coverage guarantees for unseen prompts.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: DAPRO splits calibration samples into three phases: learning a policy, conformal risk control, and deployment. It uses trajectory scores to determine continuation probabilities, reduces the variance of weighted miscoverage under the expected budget, then calibrates quantiles with inverse probability weights, and at test time only looks at the initial prompt.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: On Toxicity, target coverage 90%, per-sample budget 20, the authors claim the average deviation over four models is 1.90× lower than static and variance is 3.32× lower. For Red-Team's Phi-4 Mini, the full event rate is 79.6%, with the lowest estimates being static 66.6% and DAPRO 73.7%.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors note that in the experiments CRC often does not use up the budget, the coverage guarantee depends on calibration and test data being identically distributed, and τ̂ does not vary with the test prompt. The experiments include Toxicity, Red-Team, AutoIF, and an appendix hallucination task, with the target models being the 4 listed in the main text; the main text does not give the original coverage values for each model in Figure 2.

titleEn: The paper proposes LPCI: prompt control injection attacks targeting the agent logic layer and persistent memory.
summary: The paper proposes Logic-layer Prompt Control Injection (LPCI), a class of attacks targeting the logic execution layer and persistent memory of agent systems. title: When Persuasion Overrides Truth in Multi-Agent LLM Debates: Introducing a Confidence-Weighted Persuasion Override Rate (CW-POR)
titleEn: The study proposes the CW-POR metric to measure persuasion coverage in multi-agent LLM debates.
summary: The paper proposes Confidence-Weighted Persuasion Override Rate (CW-POR) to measure how often a judge LLM is persuaded by incorrect arguments in multi-agent debate and how confident it is in the wrong option. The study uses a single-round multi-agent debate framework: one LLM-based agent gives the truthful answer from TruthfulQA, another agent argues for the incorrect claim, and the same LLM architecture serves as judge. Experiments cover five open-source LLMs (3B to 14B parameters) and systematically vary agent utterance length (30 to 300 words). Results show that even smaller models can construct persuasive arguments that override truthful answers, often with high confidence. The authors argue this highlights the need for robust calibration and adversarial testing to prevent LLMs from confidently endorsing misinformation.

parts.text: When an LLM both generates and judges, neutral facts and forceful incorrect statements seen in a single round may conflict. The authors aim to measure together how often the judge is persuaded and how confident it is when choosing wrong.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: On the TruthfulQA validation split, the same model family plays the roles of neutral explanation, erroneous defense, and judge. The judge reads both sides randomly and scores 1–5. CW-POR weights incorrect choices using normalized self-assessment multiplied by LLC, with lengths ranging from 30 to 300 words.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: Across five 3B–14B models, the authors claim that confident misjudgment is least likely around 90–120 words, with trends diverging after longer lengths. Most models have higher CW-POR on non-adversarial questions; Phi-4 14B still shows high textual confidence when choosing incorrectly. The main text does not include specific percentages.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors propose expanding categories with high CW-POR and few samples, adding limited rebuttals, using judges of different architectures, and applying thresholds or external verification when combined confidence is high. This run covers five models, triangular same-family, single-round; the paper does not report the number of questions or repetitions.

title: Prompt-in-Content Attacks: Exploiting Uploaded Inputs to Hijack LLM Behavior
titleEn: Prompt-in-Content attacks: hijacking LLM behavior using uploaded input
summary: The paper proposes a new class of attack called prompt in content injection, which embeds adversarial instructions in seemingly benign uploaded documents or pasted text. After the LLM processes them, it can generate biased summaries, fabricated claims, or misleading advice, without user awareness and without the system being compromised. The authors verified the feasibility of the attack on multiple mainstream platforms, analyzed its root cause as insufficient prompt concatenation and input isolation, and discussed mitigation strategies.

parts.text: Commercial LLMs often concatenate the uploaded document and the user query into the same prompt. A third party can embed instructions in a seemingly normal file, and when the user performs an ordinary task such as summarization, the model may rewrite, refuse, or deflect the output without the user's knowledge.
parts.label: Questions

parts.text: The authors define the prompt-in-content attack: the attacker pre-writes a single natural-language instruction in the middle of a document, without touching the model interface or using jailbreaks. The four goal types are task suppression, output replacement, behavior redirection, and framework manipulation. The evaluation uploads .docx files on the default web interfaces of seven services and observes the outputs.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: The authors state that most platforms execute embedded instructions. Table 1: Grok 3, DeepSeek R1, and Kimi were successful across all four types; Claude Sonnet4 and ChatGPT 4o blocked all four types. Grok 3 also placed the previously mentioned password into a redirect link (Figure 5).
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors limited themselves to single-turn public web interfaces and did not examine multi-turn persistence, long-term memory leakage, or account-linked poisoning; the exfiltration test was in a controlled environment and did not use real user data. summary: The paper proposes MARGIN (Multi-Agent Runtime Grading via Incremental Normalisation), a runtime calibration method that learns model-specific confidence corrections from observed answer outcomes without retraining models or a held-out calibration set. In code generation, question answering, and math evaluations on an 18-model pool and a 9-model subset, MARGIN achieved lower post-transfer expected calibration error than all five online calibration baselines on two code generation transfers, and lower than four on the question answering transfer. In code generation coordination experiments, calibration improved answer selection accuracy on two benchmarks by 4.3 and 14.0 percentage points, respectively.

parts.text: The coordinator needs to compare answers from heterogeneous base models using self-reported confidence; the same score means different things across models, and after the task distribution changes the old correction may also no longer apply. parts.label: Questions

parts.text: Within each model's confidence bands, MARGIN tracks accuracy and self-reported confidence with an EWMA, corrects scores by their ratio, and shrinks sparse bands toward that model's overall ratio. The corrected scores serve as voting weights for the answers already obtained. No retraining, no access to internal state, no separate calibration set, but it depends on subsequent correctness feedback.
parts.label: Methods

parts.text: After two code transfers, nine-cloud MARGIN achieves ECE of 12.99 and 11.89, lower than the five online baselines; MMLU-shift is 2.85, inconclusive compared with online Platt. The 18-model cold-start selection accuracy improves by 4.32 and 13.98 percentage points on MBPP and BCB.
parts.label: Experiments and results

parts.text: The authors state that applicability depends on correctness feedback; verifying only the selected answerer harms calibration; generalization is limited by the archived queue and mutation transfer, and gradual drift was not tested. The experiments use an 18-model pool and a nine-cloud subset; question answering and math only do calibration, not voting.
